title: Comparison Operators
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behavior of comparison operators in C#.
Identify the relevant operand types, evaluation rules and result types.
Read and explain original C# code that demonstrates the lesson concepts.
Predict deterministic program output and identify common mistakes.
Compile and execute a small .NET 10 console example to verify the result.

understand.concept: Comparison operators compare two values and produce a bool result. Equality and inequality use == and !=; relational comparisons use <, >, <= and >=. Numeric comparisons follow numeric conversion rules. For strings, == compares string values using string equality semantics, while ordering and culture-sensitive text comparisons should use the appropriate string comparison APIs. Reference types may define overloaded equality operators, so == does not universally mean reference identity.
understand.whyItMatters: Comparisons drive validation, sorting decisions, eligibility checks and conditional branches.
understand.analogy: A comparison is like checking two measurements against a rule and receiving a true-or-false answer.
understand.analogyLimit: Floating-point equality can be surprising because many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly in binary. For approximate numeric comparisons, define an appropriate tolerance.

explain.narrative:
## Equality and inequality

`==` tests equality and `!=` tests inequality. For built-in numeric types these compare numeric values. For strings, `==` compares string contents using ordinal string equality.

## Relational operators

`<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare ordered values and return `bool`. They are commonly used in range checks, thresholds and loop conditions.

## Type and precision considerations

The compiler applies numeric promotion where defined. Comparing floating-point results for exact equality can be unreliable after calculations; use a domain-appropriate tolerance when approximate equality is intended. For culture-aware text ordering, use `String.Compare` with an explicit comparison mode rather than assuming `<` works for strings.

Examples target .NET 10 and C# 14.

questions.prompt: Why should a developer understand operand types?
questions.answer: Types affect which operation is selected and what result is produced.
options: Types affect which operation is selected and what result is produced.
Types are used only to change variable names.
Types never affect arithmetic results.
Types remove the need for validation.
questions.explanation: C# operations are type-aware, so the types of operands influence conversions and results.

questions.prompt: What is a good way to make a complex expression easier to maintain?

options: Use clear names and parentheses to make intent explicit.

Put every operation on one line.
